extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners applying the Mayo/Alice two-step (implemented as Steps 2A and 2B in USPTO SME guidance) to determine §101 eligibility of computer-implemented and software-related claims, using recent Federal Circuit decisions as illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole under Step 2A; avoid oversimplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider the claim as a whole under Step 2A of the USPTO's SME guidance, and should not overgeneralize the claim or simplify it into its 'gist' or core principles when identifying a concept as a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The McRO court cautioned that courts 'must be careful to avoid oversimplifying the claims' by looking at them generally and failing to account for the specific requirements of the claims. Examiners should account for the specific claim limitations rather than reducing claims to an overly broad characterization similar to previously-identified abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to an improvement in computer-related technology may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim directed to an improvement in computer-related technology is not necessarily directed to an abstract idea and therefore may be patent eligible under Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'improvement in computer-related technology' can include improvements beyond mere operation of a computer or network; it can be a set of 'rules' (mathematical relationships) that enable a computer to perform a function not previously performable by a computer. The McRO decision found claims eligible because they were directed to improving computer animation (automating tasks previously requiring human animators) rather than an abstract idea. Contrast decisions (e.g., Affinity Labs, Electric Power Group) where lack of detail as to how the improvement is achieved or mere presentation of results led to a finding of an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators that a claim is directed to a computer-related improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain facts in the specification and claim language can indicate the claim is directed to an improvement in computer-related technology rather than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable indicators include: (1) teaching in the specification about how the claimed invention improves a computer or other technology (McRO relied on such specification explanations); and (2) a claim that defines a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome (e.g., McRO's use of particular rules to set morph weights and transitions), as opposed to merely claiming the idea or outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat use of a computer as mere automation of a known human process
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely uses a computer as a tool to perform an existing process is more likely to be an abstract idea; claims that improve computer-related technology by enabling new computer performance can be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McRO distinguished claims that improved the technological process (specific rules enabling automation) from cases like Alice where a computer was merely used as a tool. Examine whether the claimed invention allows computers to do something not previously performable or improves existing computer functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination for an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is determined to be directed to a judicial exception, examiners should apply Step 2B by determining whether the additional elements, alone or in combination, amount to 'significantly more' (an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BASCOM teaches that although additional elements may be generic individually, their non-conventional and non-generic arrangement can supply an inventive concept. Example: the installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable filtering features for each end user was found relevant to eligibility. Examiners must consider combinations of elements as well as individual elements when assessing 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Mayo/Alice framework (Steps 2A and 2B) to resolve preemption questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should continue to use the MayolAlice framework (implemented as Steps 2A and 2B) to analyze whether claims preempt a judicial exception and to resolve any preemption arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant argues that a claim does not preempt all applications of the exception, the examiner should: (a) reconsider in Step 2A whether the claim is directed to an improvement in computer-related technology or a specific way of achieving a desired outcome; and (b) if still directed to a judicial exception, reconsider in Step 2B whether the additional elements in combination are more than a non-conventional/non-generic arrangement of known, conventional elements. The memorandum notes that absence of preemption has been used in some decisions to support eligibility but not in others; use the structured framework rather than preemption alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on non-precedential decisions except in closely matching factual scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should avoid relying upon or citing non-precedential decisions unless the facts of the application uniquely match those of the non-precedential decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given many recent precedential decisions, reliance on non-precedential cases (e.g., SmartGene, Cyberfone) is discouraged. The USPTO chart of court decisions indicates whether a decision is precedential or non-precedential; examiners should consult that status before citing.
